record.original_question: For low-density Euclidean random matrices in three dimensions, how can one construct a single approximation scheme that combines the strengths of the leading low-density expansion and the Gaussian variational approximation, so that it captures both the overall spectral shape and the peak produced by small clusters?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider Euclidean random matrices in three dimensions defined as follows. Let $x_1,\dots,x_N$ be $N$ points distributed independently and uniformly at random in a cubic box of volume $V \subset \mathbb{R}^3$, with number density $\rho = N/V$, and consider the thermodynamic limit $N,V\to\infty$ with $\rho$ fixed. Given a real-valued function $f:\mathbb{R}^3\to\mathbb{R}$, form the $N\times N$ symmetric random matrix $M$ with entries $M_{ij}=f(x_i-x_j)$ (the diagonal may be set to a prescribed value such as $\sum_{k\neq i} f(x_i-x_k)$ depending on the convention), and let $g(\lambda)=\lim_{N\to\infty} N^{-1}\mathbb{E}\sum_{i=1}^N \delta(\lambda-\lambda_i)$ denote the limiting average spectral density.

In the low-density regime ($\rho\to 0$), two standard approximations exist:

(A) The leading term of the low-density expansion, in which $g(\lambda)$ is approximated by the average spectral density of small finite clusters (pairs, triples, …) of points; this scheme captures sharp peaks in the spectrum generated by tightly bound small clusters but fails to reproduce the overall shape and bulk of the spectrum.

(B) The Gaussian variational (or self-consistent Gaussian) approximation, which captures the overall spectral shape and the leading orders of magnitude of $g(\lambda)$ but is unable to reproduce the cluster-induced peaks.

Construct a single, mathematically well-defined approximation scheme for $g(\lambda)$ in the low-density limit that simultaneously
(i) reproduces, to leading order, the bulk spectral shape predicted by the Gaussian variational approximation, and
(ii) reproduces the small-cluster peaks predicted by the leading low-density expansion,
and prove (or argue in a controlled way) that it converges to $g(\lambda)$ in the appropriate low-density asymptotic sense.

No clear resolution of this construction problem could be identified from publicly available sources, so the status is recorded as unknown.

status_evidence.title: Random matrix - Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: General overview of random matrix ensembles; no mention of a combined cluster/Gaussian variational scheme for Euclidean random matrices.
status_evidence.claim: General references on random matrices do not address the specific construction asked for.

status_evidence.title: Spectra of Euclidean random matrices (Mézard, Parisi, Zee, 1999) — referenced in random matrix literature
status_evidence.snippet: The foundational works introduce the low-density expansion and Gaussian variational approximations separately for Euclidean random matrices.
status_evidence.claim: The two approximation methods exist independently in the literature; no widely cited unified scheme is found.
